## In 60 seconds

A foundation model is pretrained once on many unlabeled examples and then adapted to many tasks with
few labels. For the ECG, the usual pretraining task is contrastive: two views of the same patient
should get similar embeddings, and views of different patients should not
[@sangha2024; @khattak2026; @ko2026]. Such models reached a given accuracy with far fewer labels than
models trained from scratch [@ko2026; @sangha2024], but what they learn depends on the cohort they
were pretrained on [@khattak2026]. Large language models (LLMs) are transformers trained on text;
general-purpose LLMs were not reliable readers of ECGs or pacemaker electrograms in recent studies
[@chai2026; @zeljkovic2025; @bozyel2025]. This module derives the contrastive loss and attention, builds a
retrieval step over this course's own text, and shows how to evaluate a language model's answers:
accuracy with its uncertainty, consistency, and whether its citations exist.

## From the field

- **Fewer labels for the same accuracy.** An ECG foundation model pretrained on more than 1.7 million
  ECGs with their text reports matched the best comparator's AUC in disease-detection tasks with, on
  average, 90.8% less labelled training data, in external data from another health system
  [@ko2026]. A model pretrained to match two ECG images of the same person beat ImageNet and generic
  contrastive pretraining when only 0.1% of the labels were used [@sangha2024].
- **The pretraining cohort shapes the model.** Pretraining on a multi-centre, diverse cohort
  improved in-distribution accuracy but reduced out-of-distribution generalization, because the
  model also learned cohort-specific artifacts; building each batch from one cohort helped
  [@khattak2026]. Another foundation model kept its accuracy for left ventricular systolic
  dysfunction when its supervised training data were skewed by sex or race [@hsieh2026]. Neither
  result transfers automatically to a new model or task: test it.
- **General LLMs and EP signals.** Two current general-purpose LLMs had low macro F1 for rhythm and
  axis on ECGs from a public database [@chai2026]. GPT-4 interpreted 19% of 150 ECGs correctly without clinical
  context and 45% with it [@zeljkovic2025]. On 20 pacemaker electrogram cases, ChatGPT-4o's accuracy
  rose from 57% to 66% with context but fell to 30% and 25% in the complex scenarios, where its answers
  two months apart agreed only fairly [@bozyel2025].
- **Keep data on site.** A locally run open-source LLM answered 90 of 100 questions about patients'
  echocardiogram report histories correctly, retrieving relevant snippets first; its errors included
  misread numbers and hallucinations [@vaid2024].
- **Retrieval with citations (Stanford).** Almanac, a retrieval-augmented LLM from Stanford, was
  preferred by clinicians over general LLMs on 314 clinical questions and gave correct citations for
  91% of them. When an adversarial instruction was appended to a question, the similarity between
  question and retrieved passages fell below Almanac's threshold and it abstained [@zakka2024].

## Derivations

### Pretraining without labels

Take a batch of $N$ anchors with unit embeddings $\mathbf z_i$ and $N$ candidates $\mathbf z'_k$,
where candidate $i$ is anchor $i$'s positive (for example a second recording of the same patient) and
every other candidate is a negative. With similarities $S_{ik} = \mathbf z_i^\top \mathbf z'_k$ and a
temperature $\tau > 0$, the InfoNCE loss [@oord2018cpc] is a cross-entropy over candidates:

$$
L = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \ln \frac{\exp(S_{ii}/\tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{N} \exp(S_{ik}/\tau)}
$$ {#eq-m43-infonce}

If every similarity is equal, $L = \ln N$: that is chance. The loss falls as positives become more
similar than negatives, and $\tau$ sets how hard it pushes on a given margin. Writing
$P_{ik} = \exp(S_{ik}/\tau)/\sum_j \exp(S_{ij}/\tau)$, the gradient is

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{ik}} = \frac{P_{ik} - \delta_{ik}}{N\tau}
$$ {#eq-m43-infonce-grad}

so each anchor pulls its positive closer with weight $1 - P_{ii}$ and pushes each negative away with
weight $P_{ik}$: the negatives it confuses most get the largest push. In practice the loss is averaged
over both directions (anchors from view 1, then from view 2), the embeddings come from a small
projection head on top of the features, and the features before the head are kept for downstream use
[@chen2020simclr]. What counts as a positive decides what the model learns to ignore: two
augmentations of one recording teach invariance to the augmentations; two recordings of one patient,
taken at different times, also teach invariance to day-to-day changes [@sangha2024; @khattak2026].

::: {.demo #m43-d1 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m43-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m43-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m43-d1-contrastive-embedding.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: an encoder with one hidden layer of 64 tanh units (the features) and a 16-dimensional
  projection, trained with @eq-m43-infonce averaged over both directions, $\tau = 0.1$, batches of
  128 patients, Adam with step size 0.002, for 300 steps. Precomputed by `tools/make_m43_d1.py` with
  `epml.foundation` and shipped as `demos/m43-d1-data.json`.
- Data: synthetic beats, the Gaussian-wave beat of m37 [@mcsharry2003] with patient-level wave sizes
  and QRS width, 250 samples per second; recordings differ by small beat changes, a shift of up to
  12 ms, baseline wander and noise. All ranges are illustrative, not physiological reference values.
- The scatter shows the embeddings' first two principal components at each step, computed afresh
  at each step. The probe AUC is the mean over five sets of 10 labelled patients, tested on 1,000
  others; "wide QRS" means a width factor above 1.4 (illustrative).
- What would change the result: the temperature, the batch size (more negatives), the augmentations,
  and the pretraining cohort (lab part C).
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Contrastive pretraining needs pairs, not labels; the loss is a cross-entropy whose chance level is
  $\ln N$.
- The choice of positive pairs decides what the embedding keeps and what it ignores.
- The useful output is the feature layer, judged by what a simple model can do with it.

### Linear probes and label efficiency

A linear probe is a logistic regression trained on frozen features; it measures how much a task is
already encoded. In lab part B, after pretraining on 2,000 unlabeled synthetic patients, a probe
trained on 10 labelled patients detected a wide QRS with a mean AUC of about 0.84, against about 0.63
for the same regression on the raw samples and 0.64 on the features of an untrained encoder. With
300 labels the three came within about 0.03 of each other: pretraining matters most when labels are
scarce, as in the published label-efficiency curves [@ko2026; @sangha2024; @yang2026]. In part C, an
encoder pretrained on a cohort with no wide complexes gave a weaker probe at every label budget,
and a weaker one than the raw samples once 30 or more labels were available. That is the synthetic
version of the cohort effect reported by @khattak2026.

**Key takeaways**

- Report a pretrained model's benefit as a curve over label budgets, not one number.
- Compare against an untrained encoder of the same size, so the gain is credited to pretraining.
- A cohort that lacks a feature yields an encoder that does not represent it.

### Attention

A transformer [@vaswani2017] mixes information between positions (ECG samples, image patches or text
tokens) with attention. Each position has a query $\mathbf q$, a key $\mathbf k$ and a value
$\mathbf v$, linear maps of its input. With queries, keys and values stacked as rows of $Q$, $K$ and
$V$, and key length $d$,

$$
\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt d}\right) V
$$ {#eq-m43-attention}

with the softmax taken over keys, so each output is a weighted average of the values. Why
$\sqrt d$? If the entries of $\mathbf q$ and $\mathbf k$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1,
each product $q_j k_j$ has variance 1, and the $d$ terms add:

$$
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\mathbf q^\top \mathbf k\right) = d, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\mathbf q^\top \mathbf k / \sqrt d\right) = 1
$$ {#eq-m43-scaling}

Without the division, scores grow with $d$ and the softmax approaches a one-hot choice, which
starves the other positions of gradient [@vaswani2017]. In lab part D, with 32 keys and $d = 256$,
the largest unscaled weight averaged 0.92; scaled, 0.17.

**Key takeaways**

- Attention is a softmax-weighted average of values; the weights come from query–key similarity.
- Dividing by $\sqrt d$ keeps the scores' variance at 1 whatever the key length.
- The same block serves ECG foundation models and LLMs [@hsieh2026; @ye2026].

### Retrieval

Retrieval-augmented generation puts passages from a chosen collection in front of a language model
before it answers, so that the answer can rest on them and cite them [@lewis2020rag]. The retrieval
step needs no language model. The classic method weights each word $t$ in document $d$ by how often
it occurs there and how rare it is across the $N$ documents of the collection [@sparckjones1972]:

$$
w_{t,d} = \operatorname{tf}_{t,d}\left[\ln\frac{1 + N}{1 + \operatorname{df}_t} + 1\right]
$$ {#eq-m43-tfidf}

where $\operatorname{tf}_{t,d}$ counts $t$ in $d$ and $\operatorname{df}_t$ counts the documents
containing $t$ (this "smoothed" form never divides by zero). Documents and the question become
vectors of these weights, and documents are ranked by cosine similarity:

$$
\cos(\mathbf a, \mathbf b) = \frac{\mathbf a^\top \mathbf b}{\lVert\mathbf a\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf b\rVert}
$$ {#eq-m43-cosine}

Dense retrievers replace word counts with learned embeddings, trained with the loss of
@eq-m43-infonce on matched pairs of texts; NV-Embed from NVIDIA is one such text-embedding model
[@lee2025nvembed], and Almanac used a commercial embedding model with a cosine threshold below which it
returned no passage [@zakka2024]. Whatever the retriever, measure its recall on questions written by
someone else.

::: {.demo #m43-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m43-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m43-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m43-d2-glossary-retrieval.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Method: @eq-m43-tfidf with raw counts and the smoothed inverse document frequency, rows scaled to
  unit length, ranked by @eq-m43-cosine. Text is lower-cased and split into words of letters and
  digits; a short list of stop words is removed, and a crude rule drops plural endings. The scores
  are exact for this method; the JavaScript is tested against `epml.retrieval`.
- Corpus: the course glossary and formula sheet at build time (`demos/m43-d2-corpus.json`, written by
  `tools/make_m43_d2.py`). Test questions: 24 plain-language questions written for the course; the
  same author wrote many glossary entries, which makes them easier than real users' questions.
- What would change the result: a different corpus or question set, stemming, or a dense
  retriever, which can match synonyms that share no words.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Retrieval can be tested on its own: recall at $k$ and mean reciprocal rank on known question–answer
  pairs.
- Word-matching retrieval misses synonyms; dense retrieval learns them from matched pairs.
- A similarity threshold can flag questions with no good source; in Almanac it also made the system
  abstain when an adversarial instruction was appended [@zakka2024].

### Evaluating a language model's answers

An evaluation needs a fixed question set with answers decided in advance, a metric, and an
estimate of uncertainty. For $k$ correct answers out of $n$ independent questions, the 95% Wilson
score interval [@wilson1927] solves $(\hat p - p)^2 = z^2 p(1-p)/n$ for $p$, with $\hat p = k/n$ and
$z = 1.96$:

$$
\frac{\hat p + \dfrac{z^2}{2n} \pm z\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n} + \dfrac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \dfrac{z^2}{n}}
$$ {#eq-m43-wilson}

Unlike the textbook $\hat p \pm z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$, it stays inside 0 to 1 and still gives
an upper bound when $k = 0$. To plan a benchmark, the number of independent questions for an interval
of half-width about $h$ around an accuracy near $p$ is

$$
n \approx \frac{z^2\,p(1-p)}{h^2}
$$ {#eq-m43-questions}

which is 385 questions for $\pm 5$ percentage points at $p = 0.5$. With 150 ECGs, an accuracy near
19% has a 95% Wilson interval of about 13% to 26% (our calculation, taking 28 of 150 for the 19%
reported by @zeljkovic2025 and treating the ECGs as independent).

Accuracy is not enough for a model that samples its words:

- **Consistency.** Ask each question several times, or months apart, and report agreement with
  Cohen's kappa ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa)); @bozyel2025 found only fair
  agreement for complex electrogram cases.
- **Citations.** Check that every cited source exists and says what is claimed, by resolving its DOI
  or PMID; general LLMs have cited non-existent pages [@zakka2024].
- **Breadth.** Clinical work is more than exam questions. MedHELM, from Stanford, evaluated nine LLMs
  on 35 benchmarks covering 121 clinical tasks, and found the lowest scores in administration and
  workflow tasks; its panel of three LLM judges agreed with clinicians (intraclass correlation 0.47)
  about as well as clinicians agreed with each other (0.43) on two benchmarks [@bedi2025medhelm].

**Key takeaways**

- Report accuracy with an interval; 20 cases cannot separate 60% from 80% accuracy.
- Measure consistency across repeats and check every citation.
- A model judge must itself be validated against clinicians, task by task.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where these methods could enter EP practice.** ECG foundation models are studied for screening
and risk prediction from the 12-lead ECG [@ko2026; @hsieh2026; @yang2026], building on the AI-ECG
work of m37. LLMs are studied as readers of ECGs and device electrograms
[@chai2026; @zeljkovic2025; @bozyel2025], and as tools for querying a patient's report history on site [@vaid2024]. A review
describes the evidence for cardiovascular foundation models as promising but unevenly validated, and
lists interpretability, under-representation of populations, regulatory uncertainty and workflow
integration as open problems [@ye2026].

**What the evidence is.** The foundation-model studies here are retrospective, some with external
validation [@ko2026; @sangha2024; @hsieh2026]; one is a preprint [@yang2026]. The LLM studies are
benchmarks on curated cases. We found no randomized trial of an ECG foundation model or an LLM in EP
among them. Results are reported in the papers' own units (AUC, accuracy, kappa) and none is
evidence of patient benefit (m45).

In the terms of this module:

- **Check the cohort.** Which patients, devices and centres were in pretraining, and does the target
  population look like them [@khattak2026]?
- **Check the labels.** How many labelled examples did the reported accuracy need, and is the gain
  over an untrained baseline shown as a curve?
- **Check the reader.** For an LLM, was accuracy reported with uncertainty, with and without
  context, across repeats, and with verified citations?

## How experts think

Before trusting a foundation-model or LLM result, ask:

1. **What was the model pretrained on?** Size, centres, devices and patient mix of the pretraining
   cohort; a diverse cohort can still teach cohort artifacts [@khattak2026].
2. **What were the positives?** Augmentations of one recording, recordings of one patient, or an ECG
   and its report [@sangha2024; @ko2026].
3. **How many labels did the result need?** Ask for the label-efficiency curve and the untrained
   baseline (lab part B).
4. **How was the LLM tested?** Fixed cases, decided answers, uncertainty, repeats, with and without
   context [@zeljkovic2025; @bozyel2025].
5. **Where do the numbers come from?** In an answer, every number and citation should trace to a
   retrieved source or a tool, not to the model's memory [@zakka2024; @vaid2024].

One sentence to keep: **pretraining buys labels, not truth; a fluent answer is not a measured one.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| InfoNCE (@eq-m43-infonce) | $L = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \ln \frac{e^{S_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_k e^{S_{ik}/\tau}}$; chance $= \ln N$ |
| Its gradient (@eq-m43-infonce-grad) | $\partial L/\partial S_{ik} = (P_{ik} - \delta_{ik})/(N\tau)$ |
| Attention (@eq-m43-attention) | $\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt d)\,V$ |
| Score variance (@eq-m43-scaling) | $\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf q^\top\mathbf k) = d$ |
| TF-IDF (@eq-m43-tfidf) | $w = \operatorname{tf}\,[\ln((1+N)/(1+\operatorname{df})) + 1]$ |
| Cosine (@eq-m43-cosine) | $\mathbf a^\top\mathbf b / (\lVert\mathbf a\rVert\lVert\mathbf b\rVert)$ |
| Wilson interval (@eq-m43-wilson) | Roots in $p$ of $(\hat p - p)^2 = z^2 p(1-p)/n$ |
| Questions needed (@eq-m43-questions) | $n \approx z^2 p(1-p)/h^2$; 385 for $\pm 0.05$ at $p = 0.5$ |

**Studies in this module**

| Study | What was done | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @ko2026 | ECG and report contrastive pretraining, many downstream tasks | Retrospective, external data set |
| @sangha2024 | Same-patient ECG-image pairs as positives | Retrospective, external cohorts |
| @khattak2026 | Effect of pretraining cohort on transfer | Retrospective, cohorts from four continents |
| @hsieh2026 | Foundation model under skewed training demographics | Retrospective, external test |
| @yang2026 | Pediatric-dominant pretraining, transfer to adults | Preprint |
| @chai2026, @zeljkovic2025 | General LLMs reading ECG images | Benchmarks |
| @bozyel2025 | ChatGPT-4o reading pacemaker electrograms | Benchmark, 20 cases |
| @vaid2024 | Local LLM over echo report histories | Feasibility, 100 questions |
| @zakka2024 | Retrieval-augmented clinical answers with citations | Clinician-graded benchmark |
| @bedi2025medhelm | Holistic LLM evaluation on clinical tasks | Benchmark suite |

**Rules of thumb**

- Pretraining helps most when labels are few; show the curve.
- Retrieval quality caps answer quality: test it on its own.
- 95% intervals on small benchmarks are wide; plan the number of questions first.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Write the InfoNCE loss and explain what the temperature and the negatives do.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$L = -\frac1N\sum_i \ln\big(e^{S_{ii}/\tau}/\sum_k e^{S_{ik}/\tau}\big)$ (@eq-m43-infonce): a
cross-entropy that asks each anchor to pick its positive among $N$ candidates. The other $N-1$
candidates are the negatives; more negatives make the task harder and the chance level $\ln N$
higher. A small $\tau$ sharpens the softmax, so the loss concentrates on the negatives most similar to
the anchor (@eq-m43-infonce-grad) and rewards larger margins; too small can make training unstable.

</details>

**Q2. Why does contrastive pretraining help most when labels are scarce?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The pretrained features already separate patients by the factors that vary between them, so a
simple probe needs few labels to find the direction that matters. With many labels, a model trained
from scratch can learn those factors itself, and the gap closes. Lab part B shows this: about 0.84
against 0.63 AUC with 10 labels, within about 0.03 with 300. Published curves show the same shape
[@sangha2024; @ko2026].

</details>

**Q3. For ECGs, what can count as a positive pair, and why does the choice matter?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Two augmentations of one recording (noise, gain, baseline shifts), two recordings of the same patient
at different times [@sangha2024; @khattak2026], or an ECG and its text report [@ko2026]. The model
learns to ignore whatever differs within a pair. Augmentations teach invariance only to what you
simulate; same-patient pairs also teach invariance to day-to-day variation but preserve stable
patient traits. Demo m43-d1 shows same-patient pairs pulling a patient's recordings closer than
augmentation pairs do.

</details>

**Q4. How can a more diverse pretraining cohort make a model generalize worse?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

If cohorts differ in recording devices or processing, the easiest way to tell patients apart within a
mixed batch can be the cohort itself, so the model encodes cohort artifacts. @khattak2026 found that a
multi-centre, diverse pretraining cohort improved in-distribution accuracy but reduced
out-of-distribution generalization, and that building each batch from a single cohort helped.

</details>

**Q5. Why does attention divide by the square root of the key length?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For query and key entries independent with mean 0 and variance 1, $\mathbf q^\top\mathbf k$ has
variance $d$ (@eq-m43-scaling). Without scaling, scores grow with $d$, the softmax becomes nearly
one-hot, and gradients through the other positions vanish. Dividing by $\sqrt d$ keeps the variance
at 1 [@vaswani2017].

</details>

**Q6. What is a linear probe, and why use one to evaluate a foundation model?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A linear classifier trained on frozen features. It measures what the features already encode rather
than what a large fine-tuned network can learn on top of them, so it isolates the value of
pretraining. Compare it with the same probe on an untrained encoder of the same size, and repeat it
over several label budgets.

</details>

**Q7. Design an evaluation of an LLM that reads pacemaker electrograms.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Fix a set of cases with answers agreed by experts in advance, kept out of public view to limit
contamination. Score each predefined feature and the overall interpretation; report accuracy with a
Wilson interval (@eq-m43-wilson) and plan the number of cases (@eq-m43-questions). Test with and
without clinical context, repeat over time and report kappa, as @bozyel2025 did. Report "no answer"
separately from wrong answers, and break results down by case difficulty.

</details>

**Q8. A vendor says its LLM "reads ECGs at cardiologist level". What do you ask?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

On which cases, chosen how, labelled by whom; what metric (macro F1 across rhythm classes, not only
overall accuracy, since rare rhythms are where general LLMs struggled [@chai2026]); with what
interval; with or without clinical context, which changed GPT-4's accuracy from 19% to 45%
[@zeljkovic2025]; how consistent across repeats; and on what external data.

</details>

**Q9. Explain retrieval-augmented generation and two ways it can fail.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Retrieve passages from a chosen collection, then ask the model to answer from them and cite them
[@lewis2020rag]. It fails when retrieval misses the right passage (word mismatch, as in lab part E,
or a passage split badly), and when the model ignores or misreads the passage. A similarity threshold
on retrieved passages can flag that nothing relevant was found; in Almanac, an appended adversarial
instruction pushed the scores below the threshold and the system abstained [@zakka2024].

</details>

**Q10. How would you check the citations in a model's answer automatically?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Require identifiers (DOI or PMID), resolve each one against the registry, compare title and authors,
and flag anything that does not resolve. Then check, by retrieval or by a person, that the cited
passage supports the sentence. Report the share of valid citations, as @zakka2024 did (91% for
Almanac). Lab part F plants an invented key and checks that the harness finds it.

</details>

**Q11. Why might a hospital run a language model locally, and what still needs checking?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

So that patient data do not leave the site: @vaid2024 ran an open-source LLM locally over
echocardiogram reports. Still to check: accuracy on the hospital's own questions, misread numbers and
hallucinations (the main error sources there), consistency, and access controls and logging.

</details>

**Q12. Can an LLM judge replace clinicians for grading free-text answers?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Only where it has been validated. In MedHELM a panel of three LLM judges agreed with clinicians about
as well as clinicians agreed with each other (intraclass correlation 0.47 against 0.43), on two
benchmarks [@bedi2025medhelm]. That supports using it for those tasks with periodic human audits, not
for any task without checking.

</details>

**Q13. How many questions does a benchmark need to estimate an accuracy within ±5 percentage points?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

About $z^2 p(1-p)/h^2$ independent questions (@eq-m43-questions): 385 at $p = 0.5$, 246 at
$p = 0.8$. Questions grouped by patient or case are not independent, so more are needed (the design
effect of m35).

</details>

## Code lab

The lab pretrains a small ECG-beat encoder without labels, measures what it buys with few labels,
shows how the pretraining cohort matters, checks why attention divides by $\sqrt d$, retrieves from
this course's own text, and builds an offline harness for evaluating language-model answers.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | The contrastive loss and its gradient by hand (@eq-m43-infonce, @eq-m43-infonce-grad) | numbers |
| B | Pretrain without labels, then a linear probe with 10 to 300 labels | synthetic beats |
| C | An encoder whose pretraining cohort had no wide QRS | synthetic beats |
| D | Attention and the square root of $d$ (@eq-m43-attention, @eq-m43-scaling) | random numbers |
| E | Retrieval over the glossary and formula sheet (@eq-m43-tfidf, @eq-m43-cosine) | course text |
| F | An evaluation harness: interval, consistency, citations (@eq-m43-wilson, @eq-m43-questions) | scripted stand-in |
| G | Pretraining on unlabeled PTB-XL beats, then a 10-record probe | PTB-XL (download) |
| H | Optional: the same pretraining with a 1-D CNN in PyTorch | synthetic beats |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m43_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m43_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m43_lab.ipynb).
- **Data:** synthetic beats and course text, plus lead I of PTB-XL 1.0.3 [@wagner2020] in part G
  (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; downloaded and checked against the published SHA-256 list,
  skipped without internet access).
- **No external AI service.** The language model in part F is a scripted stand-in with faults we
  planted, so the numbers test the harness, not any model. An optional cell lets you plug in your own
  model; it is skipped in CI and must never receive patient data.
- **Part H** runs only if PyTorch is installed.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A batch has 64 anchors and every similarity is the same. What is the InfoNCE loss?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\ln 64 \approx 4.16$ (@eq-m43-infonce): chance level.

</details>

**S2. Keys have length 64 with independent, unit-variance entries, as do queries. What is the variance
of a raw score, and of a scaled one?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

64 and 1 (@eq-m43-scaling).

</details>

**S3. A word appears in every one of 100 documents. What is its inverse document frequency in
@eq-m43-tfidf?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\ln(101/101) + 1 = 1$, the smallest possible: the word cannot tell documents apart, so it only
contributes through its count.

</details>

**S4. A model answers 18 of 20 questions correctly. Roughly what is the 95% Wilson interval?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 0.70 to 0.97 (@eq-m43-wilson): 20 questions say little.

</details>

**S5. What is the cosine similarity between a vector and three times itself?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1 (@eq-m43-cosine): cosine ignores length.

</details>

**S6. True or false: a model that gives the same answer three times in a row is probably right.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. Consistency and accuracy are different measurements; a deterministic retriever in lab part F
is perfectly consistent and still wrong on a third of the questions.

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Same-patient positives.** Khattak and colleagues, Figure 7: two ECGs from each patient, augmented
  and encoded; the loss pulls a patient's embeddings together and pushes other patients' apart
  [@khattak2026; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537565/)]. Compare
  with @eq-m43-infonce and demo m43-d1.
- **Embeddings that cluster by cohort.** The same paper, Figure 4: a model pretrained with random
  mixed-cohort batches forms clusters by cohort, and Figure 5 shows the clusters fade with
  single-cohort batches [@khattak2026; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537565/)].
  This module: lab part C and interview question Q4.
- **The experimental design.** The same paper, Figure 1: five pretrained models, each probed on
  five labelled cohorts, 25 evaluations in all. A good template for testing transfer.
